title: Handoff
description: `<root>/.claude/exchange/handoffs/<id>.json`. Addressed to a scope - a repo and optionally paths - or to one live session, never to a hand-typed lane name. That is the point: a lane vocabulary drifts, nothing says when it has, and the label in a script then has to agree with the label in a file nobody diffs. Two real handoffs were invisible for 9 and 3 days to exactly that. Scope addressing also works for a session that does not exist yet. Written once by the sender and never again: status lives in `handoffs/<id>/`, one file per change, per transition.schema.json. This file carried `status` and `history` until #44; because `additionalProperties` is false, a record written before that change is now refused by name rather than half-read, which is the intended direction for that breakage to travel.

id.description: Also the filename, so constrained the same way a session_id is.

from.description: Who posted it. `session_id` is absent on an imported entry, because the session that wrote it is long gone.

to.description: Exactly one addressing mode. A scope reaches whoever is working there, now or later; a session_id names the one session it was written for. Naming, not access control, and this sentence used to claim otherwise - it said a session_id reaches "one live session and nobody else", which nothing enforced on either side: `handoff list` shows every handoff under the root whatever its addressing, and `set_status` never reads this block. #45 asked which half was the bug and the answer is this sentence. A session id is not an identity, and a session that has ended cannot close its own handoffs, so enforcing the claim would strand exactly the handoffs that most need moving on - permanently open, unreachable, counted in `show`'s "N not closed" forever. So: any session may accept or close any handoff, and `by` in the transition file records which one did. The first draft of this sentence said `history[].by`, which is the field #44 deleted two commits earlier and which line 5 of this file says is now refused by name - a sentence in the contract pointing at a mechanism nothing implements. A post to a session id no live session holds says so at the time, because that is the last moment anyone is looking.

paths.description: Narrows the scope within the repo. Absent means the whole repo.

body.description: Markdown. Never parsed for structure by anything.

imported.description: Present only on an entry lifted out of a markdown ledger, and together these fields are the importer's natural key. Deliberately not a hash of the entry text: the source convention has the recipient edit the entry in place, so the text changes on acknowledgement while the identity does not. A hash key is idempotent under the operation that does not matter and duplicates under the only one that does, leaving the stale copy beside the new one still marked open.

route.description: Normalised: case folded, and the whitespace around `/`, `&` and `+` collapsed, because the same label occurs both spaced and unspaced in the source and both spellings are current. The normaliser must also tolerate a reversed arrow - one historical record names the recipient first, and no direction-bound pattern catches it.

headline.description: The original headline, normalised and truncated to a prefix. Read from the whole entry block rather than the header line, because a preserved original can wrap onto following lines. This is the component that makes the key survive acknowledgement by construction: the convention's entire purpose is to preserve the original verbatim behind a `Was:` marker, so it is the one thing the operation is defined to keep. A prefix rather than the full string, so a later typo fix does not re-key an existing entry.

date.description: Optional, and the key degrades rather than faults without it: dated entries are universal in the live file only, and two historical records carry no date at all. Route and date alone are not unique either - nine collisions across the 45 historical records, because two handoffs between the same pair on the same day is ordinary. Position is not structure here: the date is read as the first date-shaped run in the header, which is convention rather than syntax, and nothing stops a closure date being written ahead of the original.
